questions.prompt: A guidebook wants to describe "streets paved with marble" in fewer words. Which phrase does it print?

options.text: marbles-paved streets
paved-marble streets
marble-paving streets
marble-paved streets

questions.explanation: Compress a clause into a compound adjective by putting the noun first and the past participle after it, joined by a hyphen: streets paved with marble become marble-paved streets. The order cannot be turned round — "paved-marble" would describe marble, not streets. The noun inside stays singular, so "marbles" is wrong however much marble there is. And the -ing form would make the streets do the paving instead of receiving it.

questions.prompt: Four visitors ask about tonight's show. Match each question with the line of the leaflet that answers it.

options.text: How much will it cost for my ten-year-old sister?
Where exactly do we all gather before we start?
Will we just sit and listen?
Can we get something to drink there?
Meet in the main foyer at 10.45.
Refreshments served in the interval.
Children under 14: £4.95.
An interactive talk — bring your questions.

questions.explanation: A price list answers a question about money only once you have found the right category: a sister of ten falls under "children under 14", so £4.95 is her price. The foyer is the entrance hall, so a line naming it answers "where exactly" — it is the meeting point, not the room where the show happens. Interactive means the audience takes part instead of only watching, which is exactly what "will we just sit and listen?" is asking. And refreshments are the drinks, served here in the interval — the pause in the middle of the performance.

questions.prompt: The leaflet prints "Youth Arts Party, 7–9 pm". What do the letters pm stand for, and what do they tell you?

options.text: ante meridiem — before midday
post meridiem — after midday
post meridiem — after midnight
post meridiem — at exactly twelve o'clock

questions.explanation: Both letters come from Latin and both turn on the same point, midday — meridiem. The p of pm is post, after, so a party from 7 to 9 pm runs in the evening; ante meridiem, before midday, is what am means, and it is the pair everyone mixes up. Counting from midnight instead of midday would make 7 pm the middle of the morning, and reading pm as the single instant of twelve o'clock empties the letters of their work: they label a whole half of the day, not one minute of it.

questions.prompt: A review reads: "Frears is adept at the long, quiet shot, and the script tackles a subject most directors avoid." Which reading of the sentence is right?

options.text: Frears is skilful at filming still scenes, and the script takes on a hard subject
Frears prefers silent films, and the script keeps well away from a difficult subject
Frears is still learning to film, and the script argues with its own subject
Frears is skilful at editing sound, and the script picks an easy, safe subject

questions.explanation: Three review words carry the whole sentence. To be adept at something is to be skilful at it, so the reviewer is praising a craftsman, not describing a beginner. A shot is one scene as the camera filmed it, which is why a long, quiet shot is a still, unhurried scene — nothing to do with silence, and nothing to do with sound. And to tackle a subject is to take on a difficult one instead of avoiding it, so the verb says the exact opposite of keeping away from it.

questions.prompt: Your group leader goes round the table and asks each member for an opinion of the film, not a fact about it. Which answer does what she asked?

options.text: The film lasts one hour and forty minutes.
Stephen Frears directed it in 2006.
I found the ending far too quiet.
It is showing at the IMAX until Sunday.

questions.explanation: An opinion is a statement somebody else can disagree with without checking anything, and "I found the ending far too quiet" is exactly that — another member of the group may have found it perfect. The running time, the name of the director and the dates of the screening can all be checked in the programme, which makes them facts: true, useful, and not what the question asked for. Notice the opening too, "I found" — an opinion usually announces whose it is.

questions.prompt: Your last lesson ends at 4.30 pm and the arts centre is forty minutes away. That day's leaflet prints: a poetry reading at 11.15 am · an exhibition opening at 2.00 pm · a drum workshop at 4.50 pm · a film at 5.45 pm. Which one starts late enough for you to be there at the beginning?

options.text: the exhibition opening, 2.00 pm
the film, 5.45 pm
the drum workshop, 4.50 pm
the poetry reading, 11.15 am

questions.explanation: Leaving at 4.30 pm and travelling for forty minutes puts you at the door at 5.10 pm, so only what starts after 5.10 pm is still possible — the film at 5.45 pm. The drum workshop is the trap: 4.50 pm looks close enough, but it starts twenty minutes before you can possibly walk in. The reading at 11.15 am and the opening at 2.00 pm are both over: am is before midday and 2.00 pm is early in the afternoon, hours before school ends.
